scenes.visual: R+L<->RL chips, hyperbola with Kd at half saturation
scenes.narration: Write a binding reaction in the direction it comes apart: the complex R–L dissociates into free receptor and free ligand. The dissociation constant, Kd, is the ratio of loose to bound, and it has units of concentration. The intuition that makes it usable: Kd is the free-ligand concentration at which exactly half the receptor is occupied. The scale runs backwards — a smaller Kd means tighter binding. The classic student error is flipping it: Kd is not Ka; lower is tighter.
scenes.slideTitle: Binding basics: Kd is the half-saturation point

scenes.visual: hyperbola morphs to sigmoid, four site Hb
scenes.narration: Everything so far assumed one site and one ligand, which gives a smooth hyperbola. The moment a protein has several binding sites that can sense each other, the curve changes shape. Hemoglobin has four sites, and binding at one changes the affinity of the others — that's cooperativity. The result is a sigmoid, an S-shaped curve that, as we'll see, is exactly what a good oxygen carrier needs.

The Hill coefficient puts a number on the teamwork. Plot fractional saturation against ligand and fit it; the slope, n, tells you how much the sites cooperate. n equals 1 means every site works alone — that's myoglobin's hyperbola. n greater than 1 means positive cooperativity. Hemoglobin's n is about 2.8, out of a theoretical maximum of 4: strong cooperation, but not perfect. Treat the Hill equation as a black box that scores how loudly the subunits talk.
scenes.slideTitle: The Hill equation and Hill coefficient

scenes.visual: BPG doorstop in T state; right shift
scenes.narration: 2,3-BPG is the body's dial for oxygen unloading. It's a small, ferociously charged anion, present in red cells at nearly one-to-one with hemoglobin, and it wedges into a central cavity between the β chains that exists only in the tense state. So it acts as a mechanical doorstop, stabilizing T and right-shifting the curve to dump more oxygen in the tissues. To reach the relaxed state, that BPG has to be expelled. Fetal hemoglobin binds it weakly, which is why the fetus runs at higher affinity.
scenes.slideTitle: 2,3-BPG locks hemoglobin in the T state

scenes.visual: CO locks R; left shift and capacity
scenes.narration: Carbon monoxide is the R-state lock. It binds heme far more tightly than oxygen and holds hemoglobin in the high-affinity relaxed state, so the oxygen still aboard refuses to release — a left-shifted curve and slashed carrying capacity at once. The blood turns cherry-red, and a pulse oximeter, which can't tell CO-hemoglobin from oxygen-hemoglobin, reads falsely normal while the tissues suffocate. The fix is to flood the system with oxygen and compete the CO back off.
